whatItDoes: Formats a date and time into more than 20 common patterns, including ISO 8601, RFC 2822, Unix timestamps (seconds and milliseconds), US locale strings, and ordered year-month-day variants. You pick a timezone and a pattern, and the output updates instantly.
whyItExists: Dates appear in many different formats across APIs, logs, databases, and UI — and mishandled formats cause subtle bugs. A formatter that shows exactly what a given timestamp looks like in different notations and timezones saves time when debugging data pipelines.
whoShouldUse: Back-end and API developers working with timestamps, data engineers transforming records, QA engineers verifying date handling, and anyone adapting dates between systems.
useCases: See how a Unix timestamp renders as an ISO 8601 or RFC 2822 string
Verify the correct format to send to a third-party API
Convert between local time and UTC for log correlation
Produce a consistent date string for a database or report
instructions: Pick an input date, either from the picker or by entering a Unix timestamp
Select the timezone to interpret the value in
Since the pattern list updates automatically, choose your preferred output format
Copy the formatted result for use in your code or document
Switch between milliseconds and seconds for Unix-style timestamps
examples: Input 1750000000 s → Locale (US): July 1, 2025 at 12:00 AM
bestPractices: Always confirm whether a timestamp is seconds or milliseconds (10 vs 13 digits)
Serialize dates in ISO 8601 UTC when storing or exchanging them
Specify a timezone explicitly instead of relying on server default
Use RFC 2822 for email and legacy HTTP headers
commonMistakes: Treating a millisecond timestamp as seconds and dividing incorrectly
Assuming the server and browser timezones are the same
Using year-first vs day-first formats inconsistently across systems
Ignoring the offset marker when parsing ISO strings that lack 'Z'
faq: Does this tool support timezones? — Yes, you can choose UTC, local, or several common zones, and the output adjusts accordingly.
How do I tell seconds from milliseconds? — 10-digit timestamps are seconds; 13-digit are milliseconds.
Is my value sent anywhere? — No, all formatting happens locally in your browser.
Can I convert a formatted date back to a timestamp? — Yes, paste a full ISO or RFC string and the tool derives its timestamp.
features: ISO 8601, RFC 2822, Unix, and locale formats

references.label: RFC 3339 — Date and Time on the Internet
